SafePyramid: A Hierarchical Benchmark for
In-context Policy Guardrailing

Jiacheng Zhang    Haoyu He    Sen Zhang    Shen Wang   
Xiaolei Xu    Yuhao Sun    Meng Shen    Feng Liu Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

In real-world applications, guardrails are often expected to identify unsafe user–model interactions according to application-specific safety policies, rather than relying on predefined risk taxonomies. In this work, we study this setting under the paradigm of in-context policy guardrailing, where guardrails predict safety violations based on policy specifications provided in context. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce SafePyramid, a safety benchmark comprising 1,000 multi-turn conversations across 10 domains and 3,000 corresponding application-specific policies, which together contain 61,699 distinct natural-language rules. SafePyramid organizes the evaluation into three difficulty levels: L0 evaluates individual-rule understanding, L1 evaluates reasoning over rule dependencies, and L2 evaluates adaptation of full novel policy frameworks defined in context. To ensure benchmark quality, we employ a rigorous multi-stage pipeline to construct and validate the benchmark. Using SafePyramid, we evaluate 10 frontier LLMs and 5 policy-configurable guardrails and find that in-context policy guardrailing remains highly challenging: even the best-performing model, GPT-5.5, exactly identifies the full set of violated rules in only 54.0%, 35.3%, and 12.9% cases on L0, L1, and L2, respectively. These results highlight the limitations of current guardrails and call for stronger in-context policy guardrails that can reliably execute policies, resolve rule dependencies, and adapt to novel policy frameworks.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) systems rely on guardrails to monitor user–model interactions and flag potentially unsafe content [10]. Generally, guardrails are built around predefined risk taxonomies with fixed safety standards [22, 15, 19]. However, in practice, the relevant risk categories and safety standards vary substantially across applications. For example, a short-video platform might want to develop a policy for youth safety, or a video-gaming discussion forum may need policies for classifying posts about in-game cheating [31]. To this end, an emerging line of research seeks to tailor application-specific safety policies for guardrails at inference time [31, 20, 9, 25]. Ideally, this allows organizations to adapt guardrail behavior simply by editing the policy specification, rather than redesigning risk taxonomies and retraining guardrails. In this work, we refer to this setting as in-context policy guardrailing. As shown in Figure 1, the core capability of a guardrail is no longer merely mapping a user–model interaction to a risk category. Instead, a guardrail must reliably execute safety policies provided in context at inference time, making safety criteria transparent, inspectable, traceable, and accountable, while remaining adaptable to application-specific requirements.

Although promising, evaluating the effectiveness of in-context policy guardrailing remains a largely unexplored and challenging problem. Recent work DynaBench [20] takes an important step by formulating the guardrail evaluation as identifying whether a user–model interaction violates a policy composed of multiple rules. However, its rules often describe general response constraints, such as “Never use emojis.” and “Thank the customer when signing off,” making the task closer to general instruction following than safety-policy execution. This raises several important gaps for evaluating in-context policy guardrailing. For example, it remains unclear (1) whether guardrails can reliably execute safety policies, (2) what distinct capabilities are required for in-context policy guardrailing, and (3) how these capabilities can be separately evaluated.

To close these gaps, we introduce SafePyramid, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating in-context policy guardrailing. SafePyramid formulates three key capabilities required for reliable in-context policy guardrailing. (1) Understanding individual rules, the most fundamental capability of determining whether each individual rule is violated by the user–model interaction. (2) Resolving rule dependencies, a capability required for handling more complex settings in practice where safety violations often depend on the joint application of multiple rules. (3) Adapting to novel policy frameworks, an important capability for handling policies that are continually updated after model training, where guardrails must adapt to novel policies provided in context rather than relying on pretrained safety priors [12].

To separately evaluate these capabilities, SafePyramid organizes the benchmark into a three-level hierarchy with increasing difficulty. L0 evaluates individual-rule understanding with decisive and distractor rules: decisive rules are paired with sufficient conversational evidence for determining either violation or non-violation, while distractor rules are topically related but not actually triggered by the user–model interaction. These rules can be evaluated independently against the user–model interaction. L1 extends L0 with exception and conditional rules to make rules interdependent: exception rules can waive otherwise violated rules, while conditional rules can make an otherwise compliant rule violated. Figure 3 illustrates decisive, distractor, exception and conditional rule with a concrete example. L2 further extends L1 by rewriting these rules under novel policy frameworks provided in context. Following CL-Bench [12], these frameworks use fully fictional concepts to prevent models from solving the task using prior knowledge or existing safety taxonomies.

Besides its hierarchical design, SafePyramid offers several key features. (1) Challenging task. SafePyramid
requires models to predict the complete set of rules violated by a user–model interaction under the policy provided in context. Instead of producing a binary label (e.g., safe/unsafe), models must return a violated-rule set. (2) Broad coverage. SafePyramid contains 1,000 multi-turn conversations across 10 safety domains, with each conversation paired with level-specific policy specifications, resulting in 3,000 policies composed of 61,699 distinct rules in total. (3) High quality. SafePyramid uses frontier LLMs, including Grok-4.1 [40], GPT-5.4 [32], Gemini-3.1-Pro [16], and Claude-Opus-4.6 [1], to construct the benchmark. We further incorporate cross-model validation and two rounds of human review by domain experts to ensure benchmark quality. (4) Compatible evaluation. SafePyramid supports the evaluation of both frontier LLMs and fine-tuned guard models through two protocols, referred to as per-policy and per-rule evaluation. Per-policy evaluation asks models to read the full policy and directly predict the complete violated-rule set, making it suitable for frontier LLMs that can output violated-rule sets. Per-rule evaluation asks models to judge one target rule at a time and then aggregates the binary decisions (i.e., violated/not violated) into the violated-rule set, making it compatible with fine-tuned guard models that cannot output violated-rule sets. We provide an overview of the SafePyramid pipeline in Figure 2.

We evaluate 10 frontier LLMs and 5 guard models on SafePyramid. The results show that in-context policy guardrailing remains far from solved: even the strongest model, GPT-5.5, exactly matches the full violated-rule set in only 54.0%, 35.3%, and 12.9% of cases on L0, L1, and L2, respectively. The monotonic performance drop from L0 to L2 suggests that current models still struggle to reliably execute safety policies provided in context. Further analysis in Section 4 shows that more structured organization of policy context improves in-context policy guardrailing. Our work makes several contributions: (1) We formulate in-context policy guardrailing as a task where guardrails identify safety violations using policy specifications provided in context. (2) We identify three key capabilities required for in-context policy guardrailing: individual rule understanding, rule dependency resolution, and novel policy framework adaptation. (3) To separately evaluate these capabilities, we introduce SafePyramid, a three-level hierarchical benchmark comprising 1,000 multi-turn conversations across 10 domains and 3,000 corresponding application-specific policies with 61,699 distinct natural-language rules. (4) We evaluate 10 frontier LLMs and 5 policy-configurable guard models, showing that current models remain far from reliable in-context policy guardrails.

2 Related Work

LLM-based guardrails. Guardrail models, such as the Llama Guard series [22, 27, 28, 29], ShieldGemma series [45, 44], AEGIS [15], WildGuard [19], Granite Guardian [34], and Qwen3Guard [36], are typically trained to classify user inputs or model outputs according to a fixed set of predefined risk taxonomies. These guardrails are effective for specific safety tasks, but their safety boundaries are largely restricted by predefined risk taxonomies, making them less suited to in-context policy guardrailing. Recent work has begun to explore policy-configurable guardrails, where safety evaluations can be guided by user-provided policies. ShieldLM [47] is an early example that supports user-provided rules at inference time, followed by more recent guardrails such as GPT-OSS-Safeguard [31], DynaGuard [20], GSPR [25], and FlexGuard [9]. However, these guardrails handle user-provided policies in substantially different ways. This diversity suggests that policy-configurable guardrailing remains an under-defined paradigm: existing methods support user-provided policies, but differ in what policy handling means, what outputs should be produced, and what capabilities should be evaluated. This highlights the need for a unified benchmark for in-context policy guardrailing.

LLM safety benchmarks. A large body of work has developed benchmarks for evaluating the safety of LLMs. These benchmarks primarily evaluate whether models refuse harmful requests [39, 38, 46, 5], avoid toxic or biased generations [13, 8], or resist jailbreak attacks [49, 30, 4, 19, 6]. While these benchmarks have been essential for measuring general safety behavior, they usually define safety through fixed task labels, harm categories, or benchmark-specific annotation criteria. Recent work has begun to make guardrail evaluation more adaptive, but still falls short of systematically evaluating in-context policy guardrailing. For example, FlexBench [9] evaluates how guardrails perform under varying enforcement regimes, from loose to strict, but it remains centered on predefined risk taxonomies rather than policy specifications provided in context. DynaBench [20] evaluates whether a user–model interaction violates user-defined instructions, such as “Never use emojis.” This is closer to instruction-following: the evaluation mainly asks whether the transcript satisfies explicit response constraints, rather than whether a guardrail can execute safety rules in a user–model interaction and identify the rules that are violated. Therefore, systematic evaluation of in-context policy guardrailing remains largely unexplored. To fill the gap, we introduce SafePyramid, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating in-context policy guardrailing.

Instruction following, rule-based reasoning, and context learning benchmarks. Instruction following, rule-based reasoning, and context learning capture capabilities closely related to in-context policy guardrailing. Existing benchmarks have evaluated these capabilities from different perspectives. Instruction-following benchmarks evaluate whether models satisfy lexical, formatting, or system-level constraints [48, 23, 42, 35], while rule-based reasoning benchmarks evaluate whether models can apply professional rules in context [18, 26]. More recently, CL-bench [12] and CL-bench Life [11] evaluate context learning: whether models can acquire and use task-relevant information from newly provided contexts, rather than relying only on pretrained knowledge. This line of work is closely related to our L2 design, where models must learn policy-specific concepts from the novel policy framework before identifying policy violations.

Despite these connections, SafePyramid differs in both task and goal. As summarized in Table 1, existing benchmarks typically cover only part of our setting: safety benchmarks focus on fixed risk taxonomies, instruction and rule-reasoning benchmarks evaluate general constraint following or rule application, and context-learning benchmarks evaluate adaptation to newly provided contexts. In contrast, SafePyramid is a safety-centered benchmark that formulates violated-rule set prediction as the evaluation task. SafePyramid further enables separate evaluation of three core capabilities: understanding individual rules, resolving rule dependencies, and adapting to novel policy frameworks.

3 SafePyramid

In this section, we first define the problem setting, then describe the hierarchical design, domains and statistics, benchmark construction, and quality control pipeline, and finally introduce the evaluation protocols and metrics used throughout our experiments. We provide an overview of the SafePyramid pipeline in Figure 2.

3.1 Problem Setting

Violated-rule set prediction task. Given a multi-turn user–model conversation CC, a conventional safety evaluation task with a predefined risk category typically requires guardrails to output a binary safe/unsafe label. In contrast, in the in-context policy guardrailing task, guardrails are also provided with in-context policy P={r1,…,rK}P=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{K}\}, where each rir_{i} is a natural-language rule and KK is the total number of rules defined in this policy. The goal is to predict the subset of rules violated by the conversation, denoted as V^⊆{1,…,K}\widehat{V}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\}. This requires guardrails to identify the ground truth subset violated rules V⋆V^{\star} among safety rules, making it a challenging rule-level set prediction task.

3.2 Hierarchical Design

We decompose in-context policy guardrailing into three core capabilities ordered by increasing difficulty: understanding individual safety rules, resolving dependencies among safety rules, and adapting to novel safety policy frameworks. SafePyramid separately evaluates these capabilities using a three-level hierarchy with increasing difficulty, from Level 0 (L0) to Level 2 (L2). Each level retains the core task of identifying violated rules under an in-context policy, while introducing one additional source of complexity. This design disentangles model capabilities and enables systematic analysis of where models fail.

3.2.1 Level 0: Understanding Individual Rules

Goal. L0 evaluates the most fundamental capability required for in-context policy guardrailing: understanding individual safety rules. Reliable in-context policy guardrailing first requires a guardrail to decide whether a single explicit rule is actually supported by conversational evidence. Without this capability, failures at higher levels cannot be meaningfully attributed. Therefore, L0 considers each safety rule in isolation, allowing us to diagnose whether models can apply individual rules to multi-turn user–model conversations. We classify L0 safety rules into two categories: decisive rules and distractor rules.

Decisive rules describe behaviors that the policy explicitly allows or prohibits, and the conversation provides sufficient evidence to determine whether each rule is violated. A decisive rule is violated when the conversation triggers a prohibited behavior, and non-violated when the relevant requirements are satisfied or no prohibited behavior occurs. For example, in Figure 3, the chatbot gives guidance on using a named person’s public social-media content without clarifying that the guidance is general information rather than legal advice, so the rule can be directly identified as violated.

Distractor rules are related to the conversation topic but are not triggered by the actual user–model behavior. They reflect practical policy settings where a full policy may contain many relevant rules, but only a subset applies to any given conversation. Thus, distractor rules evaluate whether models over-match policy text based on surface similarity rather than grounding rules in conversational evidence. For example, in Figure 3, the conversation discusses location data, but the chatbot does not recommend publishing exact coordinates, routine travel patterns, or real-time whereabouts, so the distractor rule is not triggered.

3.2.2 Level 1: Resolving Rule Dependencies

Goal. L1 evaluates whether models can resolve dependencies among safety rules, moving beyond the isolated rule checking tested in L0. In practice, policies are rarely flat collections of independent rules. Rules may depend on one another: some clauses may qualify or override others, while some requirements may only take effect under specific conditions. Such dependencies create conflicts among rules and make the final violation context-dependent. As a result, a rule that appears violated in isolation may be waived or reinterpreted, and a rule that appears compliant in isolation may become violated once additional conditions apply. To this end, L1 introduces exception and conditional rules to test whether models can revise an initial rule-level evaluation and predict the violated-rule set under interacting policy rules.

Exception rules specify higher-priority rules that override the default classification of one or more base rules under a specified context. When an exception applies, the corresponding base rules are waived or reinterpreted, and the exception may introduce an alternative standard that must be satisfied. For example, in Figure 3, the user’s impending deadline and pressure from an editor trigger an exception that waives the base rule, but the chatbot still violates the exception rule because it fails to instruct the user to halt data compilation until formal legal clearance is obtained.

Conditional rules specify additional requirements that apply when certain contextual conditions are satisfied. When a conditional rule applies, it can make the original standard stricter or require safeguards beyond what would normally be sufficient. For example, in Figure 3, the user’s research-only framing and question about including location data trigger a conditional requirement to obtain written consent, so a base rule that would otherwise be compliant becomes violated.

3.2.3 Level 2: Adapting to Novel Policy Frameworks

Goal. L2 evaluates whether models can adapt to safety policies expressed through previously unseen policy frameworks. This level simulates scenarios where real-world policies are continually updated after model training, as organizations introduce new rules, regulatory requirements, or domain-specific standards. In such settings, a guardrail cannot rely only on pretrained safety priors or familiar risk categories, i.e., it must understand and apply the policy concepts and decision criteria defined in the provided context. Therefore, L2 extends L1 by testing whether models can identify violated rules when the same underlying policy structure is expressed through a novel policy framework.

New policy framework. Inspired by CL-Bench [12], SafePyramid rewrites each L1 policy under a fully fictional policy framework with newly defined concepts, terminology, and rule semantics. The rewritten policy preserves the underlying structure of earlier levels, including decisive, distractor, exception, and conditional rules, but expresses them through the fictional framework. This design prevents models from solving the task by relying only on prior knowledge or existing safety taxonomies, requiring them to infer and apply the novel policy framework provided in context. Importantly, the fictional framework is used as a diagnostic abstraction rather than as a claim that real-world policies are necessarily written in fictional terminology. By preserving L1’s rule structure, L2 isolates the challenge of learning new policy frameworks from context.

3.3 Domains and Statistics

Domains. We select 10 safety domains with policy boundaries that commonly vary across organizations, user groups, or regulatory contexts, making them suitable for evaluating in-context policy guardrailing, which include academic integrity, content moderation, critical infrastructure, defamation, discrimination, fraud, intellectual property, privacy, sexual content, and specialized advice. These domains are adopted and adapted from AILuminate [14]. For each domain, we construct 30 scenarios, yielding 300 scenarios in total. These scenarios are then instantiated into 1,000 multi-turn user–model conversations. We provide the full list of domains and scenarios in Appendix B.

Statistics. Each conversation is paired with three level-specific policy specifications corresponding to L0, L1, and L2, resulting in 3,000 policies composed of 61,699 distinct rules. Table 2 shows how policy complexity increases across levels: L0 contains 16,114 decisive and distractor rules, L1 introduces 12,603 exception and conditional rules on top of inherited L0 rules, and L2 contains 32,982 rules expressed under novel policy frameworks. The average policy size grows from 16.1 rules in L0 to 28.7 in L1 and 33.0 in L2, while the average input length increases from 1.6K to 4.3K tokens per case. Each case contains 5.5–6.8 violated rules on average, requiring models to predict a non-trivial violated-rule set rather than a binary safety label.

3.4 Benchmark Construction

We construct SafePyramid with frontier LLMs, using them to generate candidate multi-turn conversations and level-specific policies at scale. To ensure that generated cases follow the intended benchmark design, we rely on carefully designed rule schemas, cross-model validation, and human review. Construction and validation use four LLMs: Grok-4.1 [40], GPT-5.4 [32], Gemini-3.1-Pro [16], and Claude-Opus-4.6 [1].

Conversation generation. For each scenario, we generate multi-turn user–model conversations that contain enough contextual and behavioral variation to support policy-rule construction. We use Grok-4.1 as the conversation generator because it provides strong reasoning and writing ability while maintaining high completion rates on safety-sensitive scenario generation in our pilot runs. This makes it suitable for producing controlled safety-relevant conversations without requiring manual authoring. The resulting conversations contain 12.8 user–model turns on average. We provide a detailed conversation sample in Appendix A.

Policy generation. For each conversation, we generate three level-specific policy specifications. We use GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Claude-Opus-4.6 as the generators for L0, L1, and L2 policies, respectively. This separates policy generation across models, reducing single-generator bias and enabling cross-model validation during quality control. Before generation, we design and review the rule schema for each rule type, ensuring that generated policies follow the expected design rather than arbitrary model-generated policy text. We provide detailed policy samples in Appendix A.

3.5 Quality Control

Cross-model validation. SafePyramid uses a multi-stage quality control pipeline to ensure the quality of each benchmark component. As described in Section 3.4, we use four frontier LLMs as both generators and validators. After one model generates a policy, the remaining three models serve as validators to prevent any model from validating its own output and to reduce bias.

Checklist-guided validation. To ensure high-quality validation, we formulate each validation step as a checklist-guided verification task. For each rule, validators answer a set of carefully designed yes/no questions. A check passes if the majority of validators give the expected answer, and the final rule label (i.e., violated or not) is also determined by majority vote across the three validators. In addition, validators must cite supporting evidence and provide detailed reasoning for each decision, which also helps subsequent human review. This design makes the validation process simple and auditable for frontier LLMs. Detailed quality checklists are provided in Appendix C.

Human review. After cross-model validation, we further conduct two rounds of human review by domain experts to verify the quality of benchmark components on randomly sampled cases. During review, experts check three aspects: whether the final rule labels are correct, whether the validators’ supporting reasoning is valid, and whether any rule or conversation could lead to ambiguous labels. For cases where human reviewers disagree with the validated label or identify ambiguity in the rule or conversation, we conservatively remove the case from the benchmark. On the reviewed samples, domain experts show over 90% consistency with LLM validation, supporting the reliability of the cross-model validation pipeline.

3.6 Evaluation Protocols

SafePyramid supports two evaluation protocols with different purposes. Per-policy evaluation is the primary setting: it tests whether a model can execute the full policy and directly output the complete violated-rule set. Per-rule evaluation is an alternative setting for guard models with fixed-category or binary output interfaces. It evaluates one target rule at a time, with the relevant policy context pre-organized, and then aggregates the binary classifications into a predicted violated-rule set. Without requiring guardrails to read the full rule set, per-rule evaluation is simpler than per-policy evaluation but incurs higher inference costs.

3.7 Evaluation Metrics

We use two metrics for evaluation: rule matching rate (RMR) and rule disagreement rate (RDR).

Notation. For a scored benchmark case ii (i.e., a conversation–policy pair), let Gi⊆ℕG_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{N} denote the ground-truth violated-rule set and Pi⊆ℕP_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{N} denote the model-predicted set. We define the number of false-positive and false-negative rules as

FPi=|Pi∖Gi|,FNi=|Gi∖Pi|.\mathrm{FP}_{i}=|P_{i}\setminus G_{i}|,\qquad\mathrm{FN}_{i}=|G_{i}\setminus P_{i}|.

Cases with refusal are excluded from metric computation and reported separately.

Rule matching rate. Ideally, a guardrail should exactly recover the full ground-truth violated-rule set. However, full agreement remains highly challenging for current guardrails, including frontier LLMs. We therefore report rule matching at multiple thresholds to measure partial progress toward exact agreement. For a threshold τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], we define a case-level match indicator:

mi(τ)=[max(FPi,FNi)≤⌊(1−τ)|Gi|⌋].m_{i}(\tau)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\max(\mathrm{FP}_{i},\mathrm{FN}_{i})\leq\left\lfloor(1-\tau)|G_{i}|\right\rfloor\right].

Then RMR​@​τ=1N​∑i=1Nmi​(τ)\mathrm{RMR}@\tau=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_{i}(\tau), where NN denotes the number of scored benchmark cases. In our main results, RMR\mathrm{RMR} denotes the average of RMR​@​τ\mathrm{RMR}@\tau over τ∈{0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0}\tau\in\{0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0\}:

RMR=14​∑τ∈{0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0}RMR​@​τ.\mathrm{RMR}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\tau\in\{0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0\}}\mathrm{RMR}@\tau.

Given the violated-rule sets in SafePyramid (i.e., around 6 violated rules per case on average, as shown in Table 2), we report thresholds down to τ=0.7\tau=0.7 because reliable guardrails should recover the violated-rule set with high fidelity: for typical cases, this threshold still requires over 80% agreement with the ground truth, whereas τ=0.6\tau=0.6 would already permit roughly two or more rule-level deviations. Thresholds below 0.70.7 are therefore too permissive for evaluating reliable in-context policy guardrails. We denote RMR​@​1.0\mathrm{RMR}@1.0 as the exact-match score, where a case is counted as correct only when Pi=GiP_{i}=G_{i}.

Rule disagreement rate. RMR measures case-level matching, but it does not directly quantify how many rule-level errors a model makes. Two predictions below the matching threshold may receive the same RMR outcome even if one differs from the ground truth by one rule and the other by many. We therefore report RDR, a continuous micro-averaged set-disagreement metric that captures the overall discrepancy between predicted and ground-truth violated-rule sets:

RDR=∑i=1N(FPi+FNi)∑i=1N|Pi∪Gi|.\mathrm{RDR}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathrm{FP}_{i}+\mathrm{FN}_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}|P_{i}\cup G_{i}|}.

RDR is a lower-is-better metric and equals zero only when every scored benchmark case exactly matches the ground truth. Unlike RMR, which weights each case equally, RDR gives proportionally more weight to cases with larger violated-rule sets and reflects the overall rule-level error burden.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Frontier LLMs. We evaluate 10 frontier LLMs in our main experiments: Gemini-3.5-Flash from Google [17], GPT-5.5 from OpenAI [33], Claude-Opus-4.7 from Anthropic [2], Grok-4.3 from xAI [41], DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek [7], Kimi-K2.6 from Moonshot AI [24], Doubao-Seed-2.0-Pro from ByteDance [3], Qwen-3.6-Max-Preview from Alibaba [37], Hunyuan-HY3-Preview from Tencent [21], and GLM-5.1 from Zhipu AI [43]. Each LLM is evaluated under its strongest available reasoning effort.

Policy-configurable guard models. We further evaluate 5 policy-configurable guard models: ShieldLM-14B-Qwen [47], GPT-OSS-Safeguard-20B [31], GPT-OSS-Safeguard-120B [31], DynaGuard-8B [20], and FlexGuard-Qwen3-8B [9]. These models are among the most relevant publicly available guardrail models for in-context policy guardrailing, as they can be configured with customized policies. Among them, only the GPT-OSS-Safeguard models support the arbitrary violated-rule set output required by per-policy evaluation, so we evaluate them under both per-policy and per-rule evaluation protocols. The remaining guard models are evaluated only under the per-rule evaluation protocol. The system/instruction prompts used for each guard model are provided in Appendix D.

Agent harness. In-context policy guardrailing requires models to search over rules, resolve dependencies, and aggregate rule-level set prediction, which may benefit from explicit decomposition and intermediate checking. We therefore evaluate whether off-the-shelf agentic harnesses can improve in-context policy guardrailing without safety-specific tuning. Specifically, we evaluate three agentic harness configurations on a subset of SafePyramid: Codex (v0.130.0) with GPT-5.4, Claude Code (v2.1.142) with GPT-5.4, and Claude Code (v2.1.142) with Claude-Opus-4.7. For this subset, we randomly sample one case from each scenario for each level, resulting in 30 cases per domain per level and 900 cases in total. The instructions provided to the agentic harnesses can be found in Appendix E.

4.2 Main Results

In-context policy guardrailing remains challenging. Table 3 shows that in-context policy guardrailing remains difficult even for frontier LLMs. The best overall model, GPT-5.5, achieves only 54.2% average RMR and 34.9% average RMR@1.0, with an average RDR of 19.7%. These results show that providing a policy in context is not sufficient for current models to reliably execute the policy. We provide the detailed RMR threshold breakdowns for per-policy evaluation in Appendix F.

Guardrails struggle most with novel policy frameworks. Across nearly all models, performance decreases as the benchmark moves from L0 to L2. The drop from L0 to L1 indicates that exceptions and conditionals introduce substantial difficulty beyond independent rule classification. The difficulty is especially pronounced at L2, suggesting that adapting to novel policy frameworks remains a major bottleneck. We provide per-domain performance breakdowns in Appendix G.

Per-rule gains reveal a policy-composition bottleneck. Table 4 shows that performance improves when the task is decomposed into per-rule classification, especially for guard models. For example, GPT-OSS-Safeguard-120B improves from 23.6% to 52.4% average RMR when moving from per-policy to per-rule evaluation, and GPT-OSS-Safeguard-20B improves from 22.5% to 44.5%. By contrast, GPT-5.5 shows a much smaller gain, improving only from 54.2% to 55.5% average RMR, with RDR decreasing from 19.7% to 18.1%. This contrast suggests that frontier LLMs are less bottlenecked by processing the full policy context, whereas smaller guard models benefit substantially when the relevant policy context is pre-organized. This indicates that the main bottleneck is not rule understanding alone, but also full-policy composition. We provide the detailed RMR threshold breakdowns for per-rule evaluation in Appendix F.

4.3 Ablation Study

Higher reasoning effort helps more on complex policies. Figure 4 compares GPT-5.5 under low and xhigh reasoning effort in per-policy evaluation. The gain is small on L0, where rules are independently classifiable, but much larger on L1 and L2: xhigh effort improves RMR by 5.5 and 14.5 points, and reduces RDR by 3.9 and 15.7 points, respectively. This suggests that extra reasoning budget mainly helps with complex rule dependencies and novel policy frameworks, rather than independent rule understanding.

Agentic harnesses improve in-context policy guardrailing. Table 5 shows that agentic harnesses consistently improve per-policy evaluation. For GPT-5.4, Codex and Claude Code increase average RMR from 56.0% to 58.0% and 57.9%, respectively. The strongest result is achieved by Claude-Opus-4.7 with Claude Code, which reaches 60.4% average RMR and 40.4% RMR@1.0, while reducing average RDR from 23.5% to 17.4%. Figure 14 in Appendix H further shows that these gains appear across a range of domains, indicating that agentic harnesses are especially useful when models need to track contextual requirements, verify intermediate rule classifications, and aggregate them into a consistent policy-level decision. These results suggest that designing more advanced agentic harnesses is a promising direction for building stronger in-context policy guardrails.

4.4 Cost-Performance Trade-off

Cost varies substantially at similar performance levels. Figure 5 compares evaluation cost and average RMR for frontier LLMs under per-policy evaluation. Although GPT-5.5 achieves the best overall RMR, its evaluation cost is substantially higher than several models with comparable performance. For example, DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi-K2.6 achieve average RMR scores above 52%, while costing much less than the most expensive models. Gemini-3.5-Flash provides another strong cost-efficient option, achieving near-50% average RMR at the lowest cost among the evaluated frontier LLMs. These results indicate that model choice for in-context policy guardrailing should consider not only accuracy but also the cost required to finish the task. They also suggest that better policy-context organization and harness design may be especially valuable when high-performing models are too expensive for large-scale guardrail evaluation.

4.5 Error Attribution

L0 errors are dominated by decisive rules. Figure 15 in Appendix I attributes per-policy errors to different rule types. At L0, decisive rules account for most errors across models, often exceeding 90%. This suggests that when rules are independent, the main bottleneck is not filtering distractors, but correctly grounding policy requirements in conversational evidence. Our root-cause analysis in Appendix J shows that a common decisive-rule failure is surface-cue matching: models match local keywords in the conversation but fail to check the rule’s actual scope, stance, or speaker attribution. For instance, GPT-5.5 can incorrectly treat an attributed or negated mention as if the chatbot itself endorsed the prohibited behavior. This indicates that individual-rule understanding requires more than topical relevance. Models must verify who makes the claim, whether the claim is affirmed or negated, and whether the rule’s trigger condition is actually satisfied.

L1 errors shift to exception rules. At L1, the dominant error source shifts from decisive to exception rules for most models. This indicates that models often fail to update an initial rule judgment when an exception applies. Our root-cause analysis shows that a common failure is over-triggering exceptions: models focus on one phrase that looks related to the exception condition, but miss other context shows that the exception should not apply. Once the exception is incorrectly activated, the model may wrongly flag the exception rule or wrongly waive the corresponding base rule. This highlights the difficulty of checking whether an exception is truly triggered before changing the base-rule judgment.

L2 errors increasingly involve conditional rules. At L2, conditional-rule errors become more prominent, especially for weaker models such as GLM-5.1 and Grok-4.3. This suggests that under novel policy frameworks, models struggle to decide when context-specific requirements should apply. Our root-cause analysis further shows that GPT-5.5 can handle the same conditional template in L1, but fails in L2 after the template is rewritten using fictional framework concepts. In the L2 case, the model incorrectly treats the conditional rules themselves as violated rules, instead of using them to decide whether the corresponding base rules should be counted as violated. This suggests that novel frameworks make it harder for models to keep track of the relationship between conditional rules and their base rules.

More analysis. To illustrate these failure modes in detail, we provide representative case-level root-cause analyses for decisive, distractor, exception, and conditional errors in Appendix J.

5 Limitations and Future Work

Lack of human baseline. SafePyramid does not include a human performance baseline. Although benchmark labels are validated through cross-model validation and human review, we do not evaluate how trained human policy auditors would perform on the same rule matching task. As a result, our results quantify the performance of current models against validated ground truth, but do not directly measure the gap between model performance and expert human-level policy auditing. Future work can establish expert human baselines, measure inter-annotator agreement under the same violated-rule set prediction protocol, and study how human auditors use explicit policies to resolve rule dependencies.

Limited modality coverage. SafePyramid focuses on text-based user–model conversations. However, real guardrail use cases may involve multimodal inputs, including images, audio, video, or documents, where policy violations can depend on evidence distributed across modalities. Extending in-context policy guardrailing to multimodal settings is an important direction for future work.

Finite policy coverage. Although SafePyramid covers 10 safety domains and a large set of policy rules, its scope remains finite. Real organizations may maintain policies with additional domain-specific definitions, regional legal requirements, operational constraints, and evolving internal standards. Future work can expand the benchmark to cover more domains, languages, jurisdictions, and real-world policy variants.

6 Conclusion

We introduced SafePyramid, a hierarchical benchmark for evaluating whether guardrails can reliably execute safety policies provided in context. SafePyramid decomposes in-context policy guardrailing into three diagnostic capabilities: understanding individual rules, resolving rule dependencies, and adapting to novel policy frameworks. Our evaluation of 10 frontier LLMs and 5 policy-configurable guard models shows that current systems remain far from reliable, especially under rule dependencies and newly defined policy concepts. The gains from per-rule evaluation and agentic harnesses suggest that stronger guardrails may require better policy decomposition, context organization, and rule-level verification. We hope SafePyramid helps move guardrail research beyond fixed risk classification toward explicit, auditable, and adaptable policy execution.

Ethics Statement

SafePyramid contains safety-sensitive conversations and policy rules covering domains such as fraud, defamation, privacy, and sexual content. To reduce the risk of misuse, all conversations are fictionalized and generated under controlled constraints, avoiding identifiable real individuals, organizations, or real-world incidents except for generic references required by the scenario. The benchmark is intended for research on policy-configurable guardrails and safety evaluation, not for generating harmful content or bypassing existing safeguards. Because SafePyramid uses LLM-assisted construction, generated conversations and policies may still reflect biases or assumptions present in frontier language models. To mitigate this risk, we employ cross-model validation, two rounds of human review, and conservative filtering that removes ambiguous or disputed cases. We encourage future work on safer, more transparent, and more auditable guardrail systems.
